claim: The Drosophila larval antennal lobe is an olfactory neuropil similar to the vertebrate olfactory bulb.
source: Here, we have mapped with electron microscopy the complete wiring diagram of the Drosophila larval antennal lobe, an olfactory neuropil similar to the vertebrate olfactory bulb.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of the larval antennal lobe.

claim: Uniglomerular projection neurons (uPNs) relay gain-controlled ORN activity to the mushroom body and the lateral horn.
source: We found a canonical circuit with uniglomerular projection neurons (uPNs) relaying gain-controlled ORN activity to the mushroom body and the lateral horn.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the function of uPNs based on the wiring diagram analysis.

claim: A parallel circuit with multiglomerular projection neurons (mPNs) and hierarchically connected local neurons (LNs) selectively integrates multiple ORN signals at the first synapse.
source: A second, parallel circuit with multiglomerular projection neurons (mPNs) and hierarchically connected local neurons (LNs) selectively integrates multiple ORN signals already at the first synapse.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the wiring diagram reconstruction.

claim: LN-LN synaptic connections putatively implement a bistable gain control mechanism.
source: LN-LN synaptic connections putatively implement a bistable gain control mechanism that either computes odor saliency through panglomerular inhibition, or allows some glomeruli to respond to faint aversive odors in the presence of strong appetitive odors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a hypothesis based on the observed connectivity patterns.

claim: Odorants are detected by olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) whose axons organize centrally into glomeruli by olfactory receptor type.
source: In the nervous system, odorants are detected by olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) whose axons organize centrally into glomeruli by olfactory receptor type (Wang et al., 1998; Vosshall et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Uni- and multi-glomerular projection neurons (PNs) relay olfactory inputs to higher-order brain areas.
source: Uni- and multi-glomerular projection neurons (PNs) relay olfactory inputs to higher-order brain areas (Stocker et al., 1990; Liang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PNs target two major brain centers in both mammals and insects: one associated with learning and memory, and another that mediates innate behaviors.
source: Common between mammals and insects (Vosshall and Stocker, 2007; Su et al., 2009), PNs target two major brain centers, one associated with learning and memory (such as the mushroom bodies (MB) in insects), and another that mediates some innate behaviors (such as the lateral horn (LH) in insects) (Fischbach and Heisenberg, 1984; Heisenberg et al., 1985; Stocker et al., 1990; Sosulski et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Local neurons (LNs) mediate communication between glomeruli, implementing computations such as gain control.
source: Local neurons (LNs) mediate communication between glomeruli, implementing computations such as gain control (Olsen and Wilson, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The complete number and morphology of cell types and the circuit structure with synaptic resolution is not known for any glomerular olfactory system.
source: While the connectivity of a few glomeruli has been recently partially reconstructed in the adult fly (Rybak et al., 2016), the complete number and morphology of cell types and the circuit structure with synaptic resolution is not known for any glomerular olfactory system.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: In the Drosophila larva, each glomerulus is defined by a single, uniquely identifiable ORN.
source: In this tractable system, each glomerulus is defined by a single, uniquely identifiable ORN (Fishilevich et al., 2005; Masuda-Nakagawa et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Almost all neurons throughout the nervous system of the Drosophila larva are expected to be uniquely identifiable and stereotyped.
source: and almost all neurons throughout the nervous system are expected to be uniquely identifiable and stereotyped (Manning et al., 2012; Vogelstein et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; Ohyama et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some of the olfactory LNs and PNs in the Drosophila larva have already been identified.
source: Some of the olfactory LNs and PNs have already been identified (Masuda-Nakagawa et al., 2009; Thum et al., 2011; Das et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The output of the uniglomerular PNs tracks the ORN response in the Drosophila larva.
source: as in other organisms (Friedrich and Korsching, 1997; Nagayama et al., 2004) and in the adult fly (Bhandawat et al., 2007; Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Kim et al., 2015), the output of the uniglomerular PNs tracks the ORN response (Asahina et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in the larva and other organisms.

claim: The ORN response represents both the first derivative of the odorant concentration and the time course of the odorant concentration itself.
source: which represents both the first derivative of the odorant concentration and the time course of the odorant concentration itself (Schulze et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Gain control permits the larval olfactory system to operate over a wide range of odorant concentrations.
source: Like in the adult fly (Olsen and Wilson, 2008) and zebrafish (Zhu et al., 2013), gain control permits the larval olfactory system to operate over a wide range of odorant concentrations (Asahina et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in the larva and other organisms.

claim: The authors reconstructed 160 neuronal arbors using the software CATMAID.
source: We reconstructed 160 neuronal arbors using the software CATMAID (Saalfeld et al., 2009; Schneider-Mizell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methods used in the study.

claim: The 160 reconstructed neurons add up to a total of 38,684 postsynaptic sites and 55 millimeters of cable.
source: All together, the 160 neurons add up to a total of 38,684 postsynaptic sites and 55 millimeters of cable, requiring about 600,000 mouse clicks over 736 hr of reconstruction and 431 hr of proofreading.
evidence: This is a direct statement of quantitative data from the reconstruction.

claim: Only 0.9% of postsynaptic sites of ORNs remained as small arbor fragments that could not be assigned to any neuron.
source: Only 136 of 14,346 (0.9%) postsynaptic sites of ORNs remained as small arbor fragments (comprising a total of 0.25 millimeters of cable, or 0.5% of the total reconstructed) that could not be assigned to any neuron.
evidence: This is a direct statement of quantitative data indicating the completeness of the reconstruction.

claim: The authors sorted the 160 reconstructed neurons into 78 pairs of bilaterally homologous neurons and 4 ventral unpaired medial (VUM) neurons.
source: We sorted the 160 reconstructed neurons into 78 pairs of bilaterally homologous neurons and 4 ventral unpaired medial (VUM) neurons (2 are mPNs and 2 are octopaminergic 'tdc' neurons; [Selcho et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the classification of reconstructed neurons.

claim: The 78 pairs of neurons include 21 pairs of ORNs, 21 pairs of uPNs, 13 pairs of mPNs (plus 2 additional VUM mPNs), 14 pairs of LNs, 6 pairs of neurons projecting to the SEZ, 1 pair of descending neurons from the brain, 1 pair of serotonergic neurons, and 1 pair of octopaminergic non-VUM neurons.
source: These 78 pairs we further subdivided into 21 pairs of ORNs, 21 pairs of uPNs, 13 pairs of mPNs (plus 2 additional VUM mPNs), 14 pairs of LNs, 6 pairs of neurons projecting to the SEZ ('SEZ neurons'), 1 pair of descending neurons from the brain, 1 pair of serotonergic neurons (CSD; [Roy et al., 2007]), and 1 pair of octopaminergic non-VUM neurons ('lAL-1'; [Selcho et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the classification of reconstructed neurons.

claim: The 14 pairs of LNs originate in 5 different lineages.
source: The 14 pairs of LNs originate in 5 different lineages (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the lineages.

claim: With one exception (35a, which has 2 bilateral uPNs), the EM-reconstructed wiring diagram shows one ORN and one uPN per glomerulus.
source: With one exception (35a, which has 2 bilateral uPNs), our EM-reconstructed wiring diagram is in complete agreement with these findings (Figures 1b, 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the reconstructed neurons.

claim: Most of the larval uPNs project to both the MB and the LH.
source: Most of the larval uPNs project to both the MB and the LH (Figure 3a), like in the adult fly (Stocker et al., 1990; Luo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text, supported by a figure, and compared to previous research in the adult fly.

claim: Most non-sensory inputs to the larval uPNs are from a set of 5 panglomerular, axonless, and GABAergic neurons called Broad LNs.
source: We found that most non-sensory inputs to the larval uPNs (Figure 1c) are from a set of 5 panglomerular, axonless, and GABAergic (Thum et al., 2011) neurons that we named Broad LNs (Figure 3b,c; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the connectivity and morphology of Broad LNs.

claim: The 5 Broad LNs account for most inputs onto the ORN axons.
source: These 5 Broad LNs also account for most inputs onto the ORN axons (Figure 1c), therefore being prime candidates for mediating both intra- and interglomerular presynaptic inhibition (onto ORNs) as observed in the adult fly with morphologically equivalent cells (Wilson and Laurent, 2005; Olsen and Wilson, 2008; Olsen et al., 2010; Chou et al., 2010), and in the larva (Asahina et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text, supported by a figure, and compared to previous research in the adult fly and larva.

claim: The 5 Broad LNs are divided into two classes, Trio and Duet, based on the number of neurons of each type.
source: We divided the 5 Broad LNs into two classes, Trio and Duet, based on the number of neurons of each type (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the two types.

claim: Both Broad LN Trio and Duet provide panglomerular presynaptic inhibition (onto ORN axons).
source: While both types provide panglomerular presynaptic inhibition (onto ORN axons), the Duet makes far more synapses onto the dendrites of the uPNs.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the connectivity data.

claim: The Broad LN Duet makes far more synapses onto the dendrites of the uPNs than the Broad LN Trio.
source: While both types provide panglomerular presynaptic inhibition (onto ORN axons), the Duet makes far more synapses onto the dendrites of the uPNs. This may indicate a far stronger role for the Broad LN Duet in postsynaptic inhibition (onto uPN dendrites; Figure 3d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the connectivity patterns.

claim: In the adult fly, presynaptic inhibition implements gain control.
source: In the adult fly, presynaptic inhibition implements gain control (Olsen and Wilson, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In the adult fly, postsynaptic inhibition plays a role in uPNs responding to the change in ORN activity.
source: and postsynaptic inhibition plays a role in uPNs responding to the change in ORN activity (Nagel et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The uPNs emit dendritic outputs that primarily target the Broad LN Trio.
source: For example, the uPNs emit dendritic outputs that primarily target the Broad LN Trio (Figure 3d), indicating that the output of the glomerulus contributes more to presynaptic than to postsynaptic inhibition.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the connectivity patterns.

claim: Similar excitatory synapses from uPNs to inhibitory LNs have been shown in vertebrates.
source: Similar excitatory synapses from uPNs to inhibitory LNs have been shown in vertebrates (Rall et al., 1966)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Synapses from PNs to LNs and vice versa have been described in the adult fly.
source: and synapses from PNs to LNs and vice versa have been described in the adult fly (Rybak et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Broad LNs synapse onto all neurons of the system, including other LNs and mPNs.
source: Beyond their role in pre- and postsynaptic inhibition of ORNs and uPNs respectively, the Broad LNs synapse onto all neurons of the system, including other LNs and mPNs (Figure 1c, Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the connectivity patterns.

claim: Broad LNs may define a specific dynamic range for the entire antennal lobe, enabling the system to remain responsive to changes in odorant intensities within a wide range.
source: Therefore Broad LNs may be defining a specific dynamic range for the entire antennal lobe, enabling the system to remain responsive to changes in odorant intensities within a wide range.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the connectivity patterns observed.

claim: Broad LNs synapse onto each other.
source: Importantly, Broad LNs also synapse onto each other (Figure 3c,e) like in the adult (Okada et al., 2009; Rybak et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text, supported by figures, and compared to previous research in the adult fly.

claim: The two types of Broad LNs have a different ratio of excitation and inhibition, with Trio synapsing far more often onto each other than onto Duet.
source: Furthermore, the two types of Broad LNs have a different ratio of excitation and inhibition, originating in the preference of Trio to synapse far more often onto each other than onto Duet (Figure 3e, Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the connectivity patterns.

claim: Choosy LNs are GABAergic.
source: Another GABAergic cell type, that we call the Choosy LNs (two neurons; Figures 1c, 3c, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), contributes exclusively to postsynaptic inhibition for most glomeruli.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the morphology and connectivity of Choosy LNs.

claim: Choosy LNs contribute exclusively to postsynaptic inhibition for most glomeruli.
source: Another GABAergic cell type, that we call the Choosy LNs (two neurons; Figures 1c, 3c, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), contributes exclusively to postsynaptic inhibition for most glomeruli.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the connectivity patterns.

claim: Choosy LNs have a clear axon innervating most glomeruli, while their dendrites collect inputs from only a small subset of glomeruli.
source: Unlike the Broad LNs, Choosy LNs have a clear axon innervating most glomeruli, while their dendrites collect inputs from only a small subset of glomeruli (Figure 3c; Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the morphology and connectivity of Choosy LNs.

claim: Some glomeruli can drive postsynaptic inhibition of most glomeruli via Choosy LNs.
source: Therefore some glomeruli can drive postsynaptic inhibition of most glomeruli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the connectivity patterns of Choosy LNs.

claim: The inputs from Choosy LNs tend to be more proximal to the axon initial segment of the uPNs than those of Broad LNs.
source: Additionally, the inputs from Choosy LNs tend to be more proximal to the axon initial segment of the uPNs (Gouwens and Wilson, 2009) unlike those of Broad LNs which are more uniformly distributed throughout the uPN dendritic arbor (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the spatial distribution of inputs.

claim: In the adult fly, ORNs tend to synapse at the most distal PN dendritic terminals, allowing for some LN inhibition to occur via synapses more proximal to the axon initial segment.
source: In the adult, ORNs tend to synapse at the most distal PN dendritic terminals, allowing for some LN inhibition to occur via synapses more proximal to the axon initial segment (Rybak et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Different inhibitory LN types may exert different effects on uPN dendritic integration due to spatially structured inputs.
source: This pattern of spatially structured inputs suggests that different inhibitory LN types may exert different effects on uPN dendritic integration.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed spatial distribution of inputs.

claim: The authors found 14 multiglomerular PNs (mPNs) parallel to the uniglomerular readout by the 21 uPNs.
source: Parallel to the uniglomerular readout by the 21 uPNs, we found 14 multiglomerular PNs (mPNs; Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the mPNs.

claim: Each mPN receives unique and stereotyped inputs from multiple ORNs or at least from one ORN and multiple unidentified non-ORN sensory neurons in the SEZ.
source: Each mPN receives unique and stereotyped inputs from multiple ORNs (Figure 4c) or at least from one ORN and multiple unidentified non-ORN sensory neurons in the SEZ (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the connectivity patterns.

claim: The mPNs originate in multiple neuronal lineages and project to multiple brain regions, most commonly the lateral horn (LH) but also regions surrounding the MB calyx.
source: The mPNs originate in multiple neuronal lineages and project to multiple brain regions; most commonly the lateral horn (LH) but also regions surrounding the MB calyx.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the reconstruction data.

claim: Of the 14 mPNs, three project to the calyx itself (mPNs b-upper, b-lower and C2) and another (mPN cobra) to the MB vertical lobe.
source: Of the 14 mPNs, three project to the calyx itself (mPNs b-upper, b-lower and C2) and another (mPN cobra) to the MB vertical lobe (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the projection patterns.

claim: The authors identified an extra 6 oligoglomerular neurons that project to the SEZ (SEZ neurons).
source: In addition to the 14 mPNs that project to the brain, we identified an extra 6 oligoglomerular neurons that project to the SEZ (SEZ neurons; Figure 1c; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the SEZ neurons.

claim: A class of mPNs has been described in the adult fly but their projection pattern does not match any of the larval mPNs.
source: A class of mPNs has been described in the adult fly (Liang et al., 2013) but their projection pattern does not match any of the larval mPNs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: mPNs are very diverse in their lineage of origin, their pattern of inputs, and the brain areas they target.
source: In strong contrast to uPNs, mPNs are very diverse in their lineage of origin, their pattern of inputs, and the brain areas they target.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the reconstruction data.

claim: A small subset of mPNs has been identified via light microscopy before.
source: A small subset of mPNs has been identified via light microscopy before (Thum et al., 2011; Das et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: mPNs receive up to 26% of inputs from 5 stereotypically connected, oligoglomerular LNs called Picky LNs.
source: In addition to inputs from Broad LNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), mPNs also receive up to 26% of inputs from 5 stereotypically connected, oligoglomerular LNs that we call Picky LNs (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the connectivity patterns.

claim: Choosy LNs are GABAergic whereas at least 4 of the 5 Picky LNs are glutamatergic.
source: While both Choosy LNs and Picky LNs are oligoglomerular and present distinct axons, the Choosy LNs are GABAergic whereas at least 4 of the 5 Picky LNs are instead glutamatergic (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for Picky LNs and Figure 2 panels L-O in (Thum et al., 2011) for Choosy LNs; see also Supp. Fig. 2 of Das et al. [2013]).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing immunolabeling data.

claim: The difference in neurotransmitter between Choosy LNs and Picky LNs is consistent with them deriving from different lineages.
source: The difference in neurotransmitter is consistent with Picky LNs deriving from a different lineage than Choosy LNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the lineages.

claim: The two Choosy LNs present indistinguishable connectivity, whereas each Picky LN has its own preferred synaptic partners.
source: In addition, the two Choosy LNs present indistinguishable connectivity, whereas each Picky LN has its own preferred synaptic partners (see Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by supplementary data files.

claim: Picky LNs rarely target uPNs.
source: Additionally, unlike the Choosy LNs, Picky LNs rarely target uPNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the connectivity patterns.

claim: Glutamate has been shown to act as a postsynaptic inhibitory neurotransmitter in the adult fly antennal lobe for both PNs and LNs.
source: Glutamate has been shown to act as a postsynaptic inhibitory neurotransmitter in the adult fly antennal lobe for both PNs and LNs (Liu and Wilson, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In larva, Picky LNs may provide inhibition onto both mPNs and other LNs.
source: and therefore in larva, Picky LNs may provide inhibition onto both mPNs and other LNs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known function of glutamate in the adult fly and the connectivity patterns observed in the larva.

claim: Picky LNs present separated dendrites and axons.
source: Unlike the Broad LNs, which are panglomerular and axonless, the Picky LNs present separated dendrites and axons (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the morphology of Picky LNs.

claim: Collectively, Picky LN dendrites roughly tile the antennal lobe.
source: Collectively, Picky LN dendrites roughly tile the antennal lobe (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the dendritic coverage.

claim: About 40% of Picky LN outputs are dedicated to mPNs or each other.
source: While some Picky LN axons target select uPNs, about 40% of Picky LN outputs are dedicated to mPNs or each other (Figure 4c; Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the connectivity patterns.

claim: Picky LNs 2, 3, and 4 receive inputs from unidentified non-ORN sensory neurons in the SEZ.
source: Similarly to the mPNs, Picky LNs 2, 3, and 4 receive inputs from unidentified non-ORN sensory neurons in the SEZ (Figure 4b, Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the connectivity patterns.

claim: ORNs cluster into 5 groups by odorant preference based on dimensionality-reduction techniques.
source: Given that ORNs present overlapping odor tuning profiles (Kreher et al., 2008), we applied dimensionality-reduction techniques and discovered that ORNs cluster into 5 groups by odorant preference (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; see the Materials and methods section for more detail).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the clustering analysis.

claim: Some Picky LNs aggregate similarly responding ORNs.
source: We found that some Picky LNs aggregate similarly responding ORNs (Figure 4d; Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the connectivity patterns.

claim: Picky LN 2 receives inputs preferentially from ORNs that respond to aromatic compounds.
source: For example, Picky LN 2 receives inputs preferentially from ORNs that respond to aromatic compounds
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the connectivity patterns and ORN clustering analysis.

claim: Picky LN 3 and 4 receive inputs preferentially from ORNs that respond to aliphatic compounds (esters and alcohols).
source: and Picky LN 3 and 4 similarly for aliphatic compounds (esters and alcohols; Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the connectivity patterns.

claim: Picky LN 0 and 1 aggregate inputs from ORNs from different clusters, suggesting they may select for ORNs that are similar in a dimension other than odorant binding profile.
source: On the other hand, Picky LN 0 and 1 aggregate inputs from ORNs from different clusters, suggesting that these Picky LNs may select for ORNs that are similar in a dimension other than odorant binding profile.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the connectivity patterns and ORN clustering analysis.

claim: Each mPN responds to specific features in odor space, defined by the combinations of ORN and Picky LN inputs.
source: The stereotyped and unique convergence of different sets of ORNs onto both mPNs and Picky LNs, and the selective connections from Picky LNs to mPNs, suggest that each mPN responds to specific features in odor space, defined by the combinations of ORN and Picky LN inputs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed connectivity patterns.

claim: These features are implemented through direct excitatory connections from ORNs or indirect inhibitory connections via Picky LNs (lateral inhibition).
source: These features are implemented through direct excitatory connections from ORNs or indirect inhibitory connections via Picky LNs (lateral inhibition; Figure 4d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the circuit motifs.

claim: Some ORNs affect the activity of the same mPN through both direct excitatory and lateral inhibitory connections through Picky LNs (incoherent feedforward loop).
source: Some ORNs affect the activity of the same mPN through both direct excitatory and lateral inhibitory connections through Picky LNs (incoherent feedforward loop, (Alon, 2007); Figure 4d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the circuit motifs.

claim: The combination of circuit motifs may enable an mPN to respond more narrowly to odor stimuli than the ORNs themselves.
source: The combination of these motifs may enable an mPN to respond more narrowly to odor stimuli than the ORNs themselves, many of which are broadly tuned (Kreher et al., 2008), or to respond to a combinatorial function of multiple ORNs that describe an evolutionarily learned feature meaningful for the larva.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed circuit motifs and known ORN tuning properties.

claim: mPN A1 reads out the total output of the uniglomerular system by integrating inputs across most ORNs and uPNs.
source: For example, one mPN (A1) reads out the total output of the uniglomerular system by integrating inputs across most ORNs and uPNs (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the connectivity patterns.

claim: mPN B2 could respond to the linear combination of ORNs sensitive to aromatic compounds, but its response could change in the presence of alcohols and esters due to feedforward loops.
source: Another mPN (B2) could respond to the linear combination of ORNs sensitive to aromatic compounds (direct connections), but its response could change in the presence of alcohols and esters due to feedforward loops (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed connectivity patterns and ORN tuning properties.

claim: mPNs A3 and B3 both collect inputs from ORNs known to respond to aversive compounds or whose ORN drives negative chemotaxis.
source: And mPNs A3 and B3 both collect inputs from ORNs (Figure 4c,d) known to respond to aversive compounds (22c, 45b, 49a, 59a, and 82a; [Kreher et al., 2008; Ebrahim et al., 2015]) or whose ORN drives negative chemotaxis (45a; [Bellmann et al., 2010; Hernandez-Nunez et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is stated in the text, supported by figures, and compared to previous research on ORN function.

claim: mPN B3 receives inputs from 33a, an ORN whose receptor lacks a known binding compound, and therefore is likely narrowly tuned to other ecologically relevant odorants.
source: Additionally, mPN B3 receives inputs from 33a, an ORN whose receptor lacks a known binding compound, and therefore is likely narrowly tuned to other ecologically relevant odorants as was shown for 49a and the pheromone of a parasitic wasp (Ebrahim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to previous research on narrowly tuned ORNs.

claim: The connectivity patterns of the 14 types of mPNs are vastly diverse from each other and likely each one extracts different features from odor space.
source: The connectivity patterns of the 14 types of mPNs are vastly diverse from each other and likely each one extracts different features from odor space, often integrating inputs from non-ORN sensory neurons as well.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the observed connectivity patterns.

claim: The Picky LNs synapse onto each other in a selective, hierarchical fashion.
source: In contrast to the all-to-all connectivity of the Broad LNs, the Picky LNs synapse onto each other in a selective, hierarchical fashion (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the hierarchical connectivity.

claim: The structure of the Picky LN hierarchy suggests that Picky LNs 0 and 3 can operate in parallel, while the activity of the other Picky LNs is dependent on Picky LN 0.
source: The structure of the Picky LN hierarchy suggests that Picky LNs 0 and 3 can operate in parallel, while the activity of the other Picky LNs is dependent on Picky LN 0 (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the hierarchical connectivity.

claim: Connections among Picky LNs include axo-axonic connections.
source: These connections among Picky LNs include axo-axonic connections, and some Picky LNs receive stereotypic ORN inputs onto their axons (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the connectivity patterns.

claim: The stereotyped hierarchy among Picky LNs defines yet another layer of computations in the integration function of each mPN.
source: The stereotyped hierarchy among Picky LNs defines yet another layer of computations in the integration function of each mPN.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an inference based on the observed hierarchical connectivity.

claim: Picky LN 0 dominates the Picky LN hierarchy.
source: Picky LN 0 not only dominates the Picky LN hierarchy, and with it the multiglomerular system, but also may dramatically alter the inhibition of the entire olfactory system.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the observed connectivity patterns.

claim: The main synaptic target of Picky LN 0 is Keystone, a bilateral, axonless, GABAergic LN.
source: This is because the main synaptic target of Picky LN 0 (Figure 2) is a bilateral, axonless, GABAergic LN called Keystone (Figure 5a; Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the connectivity and neurotransmitter identity.

claim: Keystone strongly synapses onto the Broad LN Trio, a major provider of presynaptic inhibition.
source: which in turn strongly synapses onto the Broad LN Trio–a major provider of presynaptic inhibition (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the connectivity patterns.

claim: Keystone is also a major provider of presynaptic inhibition, but selectively avoids some glomeruli.
source: Interestingly, Keystone is also a major provider of presynaptic inhibition, but selectively avoids some glomeruli (Figure 5c; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the connectivity patterns.

claim: The wiring diagram predicts that two parallel systems for presynaptic inhibition can directly and strongly inhibit each other: homogeneous across all glomeruli when provided by the Broad LN Trio, and heterogeneous when provided by Keystone.
source: Therefore the wiring diagram predicts that these two parallel systems for presynaptic inhibition can directly and strongly inhibit each other (Figure 5b): homogeneous across all glomeruli when provided by the Broad LN Trio, and heterogeneous when provided by Keystone (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is stated in the text as a prediction based on the observed connectivity patterns and known synaptic signs.

claim: Picky LN 0 can promote a state of homogeneous presynaptic inhibition by disinhibiting the Broad LN Trio.
source: In conclusion, the circuit structure and the known synaptic signs predict that Picky LN 0 can promote a state of homogeneous presynaptic inhibition by disinhibiting the Broad LN Trio (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is stated in the text as a prediction based on the observed connectivity patterns and known synaptic signs.
